title: 7.7-Magnitude Panama Earthquake Triggers Tsunami Alerts Across Nine Countries
excerpt: Buildings collapsed near the epicenter, a 6.6 aftershock followed, and tsunami warnings stretched from Central America to Chile's Easter Island — while the Panama Canal kept operating.
body:
• A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Panama on Friday, centered about 10 km southwest of Pitaloza Arriba in Herrera Province at a depth of 10 km; it collapsed buildings near the epicenter, injured at least 16 people, and was felt in Panama City, Costa Rica, and Colombia.
  • The US National Weather Service issued a tsunami warning for Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, and Guatemala, forecasting waves 3 to 9 feet above tide along parts of Panama's coast; alerts extended as far as El Salvador and Chile's Easter Island. A Pacific-wide tsunami was not expected.
  • Tocumen International Airport temporarily suspended operations, though the Panama Canal Authority said the waterway is operating normally. President José Raúl Mulino mobilized the full government and urged calm.
  • US citizens in Panama are being asked to enroll at STEP.State.gov; the State Department's emergency line is +1-888-407-4747 (US/Canada) or +1-202-501-4444 (elsewhere). A magnitude 6.6 aftershock struck Friday afternoon.

The Quake

The earthquake hit just before 1:56 p.m. ET on Friday, the US Geological Survey said, with its epicenter in the southern part of Herrera Province, about 10 kilometers southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, at a depth of 10 kilometers. The USGS initially pegged it at magnitude 8.0 before revising to 7.6 and then 7.7. In Panama City, buildings shook and hundreds of visibly shaken residents evacuated into the streets; the shaking was felt in San José, the Costa Rican capital, and in several cities in Colombia.

Damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, and Los Santos, the National Civil Protection Service said. A hotel and several homes collapsed in Tonosí. In Penonomé, a cathedral in the main square partially collapsed and cracked, alongside damage to the governor's office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. The colonial-era Church of San Atanasio in Los Santos province — declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938 — collapsed. Large fissures ran along roadways in Veraguas. At least 16 people were injured, including 15 in Coclé Province; no deaths had been reported as of Friday evening.

"We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're okay, though we're very scared. Everyone is outside, scared."

— Rosendo Domínguez, 60, Herrera province, to the Associated Press

Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, several above magnitude 5. The largest, a 6.6, struck Friday afternoon.

Tsunami Alerts Across the Pacific Coast

The US National Weather Service issued a tsunami warning for the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, and Guatemala, forecasting waves 3 to 9 feet above normal tide levels in some coastal areas of Panama. The broader US Tsunami Warning System listed potential threats for Costa Rica, Mexico, Peru, El Salvador, and Nicaragua as well. Chile's government placed Easter Island — some 3,500 kilometers off its mainland — under a precautionary advisory. Officials stressed a Pacific-wide tsunami was not expected, and the National Weather Service's Los Angeles office told Californians plainly: "A tsunami is NOT expected for California from the recent large earthquake in Panama."

The timing compounded California's anxiety: parts of the Southern California coast were already battling dangerous surf and flooding from former Hurricane Rachel, with sections of the Long Beach Peninsula boardwalk collapsing Friday.

Response and Disruption

President José Raúl Mulino urged calm on X: "What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder." He said the entire government was mobilizing, and that he would personally coordinate in the hardest-hit areas. Tocumen International Airport in Panama City — which handled more than 20 million travelers in 2025 — temporarily suspended operations and activated evacuation plans, pending safety checks. The Panama Canal Authority, the linchpin of global shipping, said the waterway was operating normally and that specialized teams were inspecting facilities.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the State Department was "rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist" at Panama's request, and the US Embassy in Panama said it was accounting for the welfare of Americans in the country — Panama being a well-known retirement destination, with tens of thousands of US expatriates. Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella offered "whatever assistance is needed."

Context and What Comes Next

The last earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991: a magnitude 7.4 centered in nearby Costa Rica that killed 23 people, injured 559, and left thousands homeless in the border Bocas de Toro region. Panama sits on the Ring of Fire, where the Cocos, Nazca, and Caribbean tectonic plates interact, making quakes common along its Pacific coast and the Costa Rican border.

Authorities will give a full damage briefing as inspections finish. Travelers should expect disruptions at Tocumen until operations are cleared to resume, and coastal communities across Central and northern South America will remain under watch until the tsunami alerts are fully stood down.
